content: External inspection systems are implemented in healthcare settings to encourage adherence to evidence-based standards, with the goal of improving organizational structures, healthcare provider behaviors, and patient outcomes. These systems operate under the assumption that external oversight and assessment will lead to higher-quality care. However, the actual impact of such inspections on organizational, provider, and patient-level outcomes remains unclear. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of external inspection systems in improving the behavior of healthcare organizations, healthcare professionals, and patient outcomes. The search for relevant studies included multiple electronic databases up to June 1, 2015, with no restrictions on language or publication status. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized trials (NRCTs), interrupted time series (ITSs), and controlled before-and-after studies (CBAs) that assessed the effects of external inspections on healthcare organizations, healthcare professionals, or patient outcomes in hospitals, primary care, and community-based healthcare settings. Two studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. The first was a cluster RCT conducted in 20 public hospitals in South Africa, which examined the effects of external inspection on compliance with the Council for Health Services Accreditation for South Africa (COHSASA) standards and eight indicators of hospital quality. The study reported mixed results. Compliance with COHSASA standards improved significantly in intervention hospitals, with a mean intervention effect of 30% (95% confidence interval [CI] 23% to 37%, P < 0.001). The compliance score increased from 48% to 78% in intervention hospitals, while it remained unchanged at 43% in control hospitals. However, the median intervention effect for hospital quality indicators was modest, at 2.4% (range -1.9% to +11.8%). The second study was an ITS conducted across all acute hospital trusts in England, which evaluated compliance with policies aimed at reducing healthcare-acquired infections, specifically methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The study reported a mean reduction of 100 MRSA cases per quarter (95% CI -221.0 to 21.5, P = 0.096) at three months post-intervention, but an increase of 70 cases per quarter (95% CI -250.5 to 391.0, P = 0.632) at 24 months. Regression analysis showed no significant difference in MRSA rates before and after the external inspection (difference in slope 24.27, 95% CI -10.4 to 58.9, P = 0.147). Neither study provided data on unintended or adverse consequences of external inspections, nor did they report economic outcomes. The cluster RCT primarily focused on organizational changes and did not include patient-reported outcomes other than patient satisfaction. The certainty of the evidence from both studies was rated as very low, making it uncertain whether external inspection programs improve compliance with accreditation standards or reduce healthcare-acquired MRSA infection rates. The authors concluded that there is a lack of high-quality controlled studies evaluating the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of external inspection systems. To better understand the impact of these interventions, further research is needed across diverse settings and contexts, with a focus on outcomes that are meaningful to patients.
